chapter: Film work, recording and looking back
title: Unauthorized taping and a Bonn recording standoff
summary: They discuss bootleg recordings, and Blakeney tells of a Bonn concert where Barry Martyn won $100 for allowing taping.

story.theme_name: Getting paid for records: royalties, publishing and flat fees
story.community_name: Royalties, publishing and who owns the song

blocks.x: I think that's what prompted the musician's union to outlaw this taping on engagements, because so many musicians had been exploited, particularly black musicians, have been exploited. People would go, oh, I just want to record this, this is for my own pleasure and then some years later you hear it and you see people making money off of it. Many musicians have experienced this, and I think it still goes on to some degree.
Yes it does. I can remember one incident, we were in Bonn, Germany--

ago.
We were playing at a concert
and the hall was just packed and the movies,
T.V. stations, had all their equipment getting
ready to go up to record everything, and
Barry Martyn flipped. Barry went to talk
with the promoters to get this thing straight,
but he had told them right up front that no
recordings were to be made unless prearrange-
ments were made and the proper--

So he goes upstairs and stayed
there for quite a while. We were sitting
there on the bandstand and these Germans are
getting nervous out there and began making
a lot of noise--

I sent word up to come down
and play something because these people were

going to do something to us. (laughing) So Barry sent word, never mind, just be still, everything will be all right, but those people were stomping their feet, wanting to know when we were going to play. They paid big money to come see us. So anyway, finally Barry came down with an agreement. They were going to give us a hundred dollars cash that night just for the recording; and then I was at ease. You know the Germans, they're kind of mean--they can be. (Laughing)

When they start stomping their feet, they want to hear some jazz, they want to hear it. They really weren't too concerned about what was going to be recorded. You know it's really not--in this country and other countries--I think it's not really policed the way it should be, because they're still ripping off musicians with the "I just want it for my own personal

Now they've gotten into videotaping so now they just want that for their own personal use. Musicians will have to fight that and the taping that they see in their friends' record collections that they knew nothing about.
